exact_use_excerpts.exact_source_text: Now suppose $1\le p\le15$. Set $\Sigma_0=(M/2)I$ and $\Sigma_1=(M/2)I+h e_1e_1^T$, where $h=\gamma M\sqrt{p/n}$. The condition $p/n\le c_1$ and small $\gamma$ make both matrices members of $\mathcal F_p(M)$. With $t=2h/M\le1/2$, [F3] gives $$D(N_p(0,\Sigma_0)\|N_p(0,\Sigma_1)) =\frac12[\log(1+t)+(1+t)^{-1}-1]\le t^2/4.$$ The derivative of the bracket is $t/(1+t)^2\le t$, proving the bound. By [F4], the $n$-sample KL is at most $\gamma^2p\le15\gamma^2$; choose $\gamma$ so it is at most $1/2$. [F1, F3, F4, algebra]

Let $Q_0=N_p(0,(M/2)I)$ be a reference law. For each $W$, the relative perturbation has eigenvalues $r_i$ with $|r_i|\le1/2$ and $\sum_i r_i=0$. By [F3], $$D(N_p(0,\Sigma_W)\|Q_0) =\frac12\sum_i(r_i-\log(1+r_i)) \le\frac12\sum_i r_i^2\le2(a/M)^2p.$$ The scalar inequality follows by integrating $t/(1+t)$ from zero to $r_i$ and using $|t/(1+t)|\le2|t|$ for $|t|\le1/2$. Also $\sum_i r_i^2=4a^2\|W\|_F^2/(M^2p)$ and $\|W\|_F^2=2N_0$. By [F4], the average $n$-sample KL to $Q_0^{\otimes n}$ is at most $2\gamma^2p^2$. Choose $\gamma$ smaller if needed so this is at most $\frac1{10}\log|\mathcal W|$. [F3, F4, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

Suppose $p/n>c$ and $n<2/c$. Take $\Sigma_0=(M/2)I_p$ and $\Sigma_1=\Sigma_0+h e_1e_1^T$, where $h=M\sqrt c/4$. Both are positive definite in $\mathcal F_p(M)$ and their operator separation is $h$. Put $t=2h/M=\sqrt c/2$. The scalar KL calculation from step 1.3 and [F3] gives $D(P_0\|P_1)=\frac12[\log(1+t)+(1+t)^{-1}-1]\le t^2/4=h^2/M^2$; the bracket has derivative $t/(1+t)^2\le t$ for $t\ge0$. Thus [F4] gives $D(P_0^{\otimes n}\|P_1^{\otimes n})\le nh^2/M^2<1/8$, and [F6] gives total variation at most $1/4$. Classify an arbitrary Borel estimator by the nearer of these two covariance matrices, resolving ties by the first index. This is a Borel binary test by [F10]. Apply the expected squared-risk theorem [F7] to that test with scalar targets $0,1$: its squared risks are exactly its error probabilities, so their maximum is at least $(1-\mathrm{TV})/8\ge3/32\ge c$. A wrong classification forces the original operator error to be at least $h/2$ by the triangle inequality. The ambient maximum tail probability is therefore at least $c$ at squared threshold $h^2/4=M^2c/64\ge a_M\min\{1,p/n\}$. [F1, F3, F4, F6, F7, F10, step 1.3, step 6.1, given, algebra]

Suppose $s=1$ and $p\ge3$. For $1\le j\le p$, let $\Sigma_j=(M/2)I+h e_je_j^T$, where $h=\gamma M\sqrt{\log p/n}$. These matrices are diagonal, so [F1] places them in $\mathcal F_{p,1}(M)$. Since $\log p/n\le c_1$, choose $\gamma\sqrt{c_1}\le1/2$ so their largest eigenvalue is at most $M$. Their pairwise operator distance is $h$. Relative to $Q_0=N_p(0,(M/2)I)$, [F2] and $t=2h/M\le1$ give $$D(N_p(0,\Sigma_j)\|Q_0)=\frac12[t-\log(1+t)]\le t^2/4.$$ The inequality follows by integrating $x/(1+x)\le x$ from $0$ to $t$. By [F3], each $n$-sample KL is at most $\gamma^2\log p$. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

The remaining case with $s=1$ is $p=2$. Let $\Sigma_0=(M/2)I$ and $\Sigma_1=(M/2)I+h e_1e_1^T$, where $h=\gamma M\sqrt{\log(2e)/n}$. The sample-size condition and small $\gamma$ make both matrices members of $\mathcal F_{2,1}(M)$. With $t=2h/M\le1/2$, [F2] gives $$D(N_2(0,\Sigma_0)\|N_2(0,\Sigma_1)) =\frac12[\log(1+t)+(1+t)^{-1}-1]\le t^2/4.$$ The derivative of the bracket is $t/(1+t)^2\le t$, proving the inequality. By [F3], choose $\gamma$ small enough that the $n$-sample KL is at most $1/2$. Pinsker [F5] gives total variation at most $1/2$; [F6] then gives maximum binary testing error at least $1/16$. A wrong nearest covariance decision forces error at least $h/2$, and its decision cells are Borel by finite distance comparisons, so [F7] gives an admissible test kernel. Thus one law has probability at least $1/16$ of squared error at least $h^2/4=\gamma^2M^2\log(2e)/(4n)$, which is the required rate. [F2, F3, F5, F6, F7, algebra]

Let $Q_0=N_p(0,(M/2)I)$. The relative perturbation has eigenvalues $2a/M,-2a/M$ and zero otherwise. By [F2], $$D(N_p(0,\Sigma_\omega)\|Q_0) =-\frac12\log(1-(2a/M)^2)\le4(a/M)^2.$$ The scalar inequality follows by integrating $(1-x)^{-1}\le2$ from $0$ to $x=(2a/M)^2\le1/2$. By [F3], the $n$-sample KL to $Q_0^{\otimes n}$ is at most $4\gamma^2s\log(ep/s)$. Since $\log|\mathcal W|\ge\frac{9}{10}s\log(ep/s)/8$, choose $\gamma^2\le\frac{9}{3200}$ so this KL is at most $\frac{1}{10}\log|\mathcal W|$. [F2, F3, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra]

Put $r=\epsilon/2$. By [F4], $$D(N_p(0,\Sigma_0)\|N_p(0,\Sigma_1)) =\frac12\left[\log(1+r)+(1+r)^{-1}-1\right] \le\frac{r^2}{4}=\frac{\epsilon^2}{16}.$$ The derivative of the bracket is $r/(1+r)^2\le r$; integration from $0$ proves the inequality. Pinsker [F2] gives $TV\le\epsilon/\sqrt{32}\le\epsilon\le\epsilon/(1-\epsilon)$ for $0<\epsilon<1$. At $\epsilon=1$, the modulus threshold is infinite. [F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra]
